title: Loss-independent time-delay estimation via Hong-Ou-Mandel photon bunching detection
authors: Julián Defant, Agustina G. Magnoni, Miguel A. Larotonda, Laura T. Knoll
abstract: In this work we study the application of two-photon correlated quantum states for high-precision time estimation. To achieve this, photon pairs were fed into a Hong-Ou-Mandel polarization interferometer to generate N00N entangled states with $N = 2$. Two- and four-detector schemes were considered, and the achievable time estimation precision of each was studied, with particular emphasis on the system's Fisher information in each case. Our results reveal that using a four-detector scheme, enabling the measurement of both coincidence and photon-bunching terms, achieves the maximum precision given by the quantum Fisher information, without the need of characterizing system losses. We also show that correlations between repetitions arise due to systematic errors, limiting the precision enhancement that can be obtained by increasing the number of repetitions. Taking these correlations into account, we show that the four-detector scheme outperforms the two-detector scheme in the precision of time-delay estimation. With the experimentally determined calibration uncertainties, the four-detector scheme improves the dispersion by a factor of 2 for the repetitions performed, reaching up to a factor of 4 as both schemes approach their systematic floors.
summary: This paper demonstrates a method for highly precise time-delay estimation using entangled photon pairs in a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometer. By implementing a four-detector measurement scheme that analyzes photon bunching, the authors achieve a measurement precision limited only by fundamental quantum noise, circumventing the need to accurately characterize system losses inherent in simpler two-detector setups.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of achieving high-precision time-delay estimation using two-photon quantum states while remaining robust against system losses and calibration uncertainties.
main_result: A four-detector measurement scheme, which utilizes both coincidence and photon-bunching terms, achieves the ultimate quantum precision limit without requiring explicit characterization of system losses, significantly outperforming two-detector methods.
method: The authors employ quantum estimation theory, comparing the achievable Fisher Information from two different detector setups (two vs. four detectors) in a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometer.
model_or_system: The physical system is a polarization-based Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interferometer used to generate and measure two-photon correlated N00N states. The analysis compares measurement statistics derived from two-detector and four-detector coincidence/bunching measurements.
key_observables: Coincidence rates, photon-bunching terms, Fisher Information (FI) and Quantum Fisher Information (QFI), and the estimated time delay ($\Delta L$ or $\delta	au$).
important_parameters: System loss probability ($\gamma$), interferometric visibility ($\alpha$), and the number of measurement repetitions ($m$).
main_assumptions: The primary comparison is between ideal theoretical limits (QFI) and practical measurements, noting that systematic correlations between repetitions limit the achievable precision in both schemes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the HOM interferometer, theoretical probability distributions for the two and four-detector schemes, and plots comparing the estimated path difference ($\Delta L$) and its dispersion over multiple repetitions for both schemes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical framework using QFI, detailing the mathematical differences between two-detector and four-detector measurements, and concluding with experimental/numerical results comparing the performance and robustness of the two schemes.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems, as it provides a concrete, experimentally relevant protocol for quantum metrology that explicitly tackles the practical limitations imposed by photon loss and imperfect calibration.
